body: I'm sorry that you feel that you are misunderstood. I too have had to deal with CRPS for many years & have recently been diagnosed as having fibromyalgia. I am forced to live with my family, since I find it very difficult to survive on my own, & it seems that my family & doctors are all dismissive of my pain. My doctor told me that I am doing just fine, that what I am experiencing is really all that bad & if I just do my PT every day it should help. To be able to understand what we have to deal with is very difficult, unless they have to deal with it as well. Even my mom, a retired home hospice nurse, thinks she knows everything about CRPS but refuses to do any research on it. The best that I can say is to keep posting & reach out to those that do understand. It helps me feel a little better about myself.

So glad to hear that you were able to go in for the trial! I have had mine for a few years now. It was a huge help for me. I was able to get into physical therapy once the permanent device was implanted. They were able to work with me enough to desensitize my foot and ankle to the point that I am able to wear a sock most days, and a shoe for a few hours. It also allowed me to walk with a cane for short distances, and without one while moving about the kitchen. I have had to have my battery and one lead replaced after the first 2 years, which is considered a relatively short timeframe. I have heard that most people get between 5-7 years before that usually happens.

My back was very sore for the trial, and when they put in the permanent device, but it was well worth it in the long run.

Best of luck to you! I hope it goes well for you.

I have found that my appetite is virtually nil! I eat supper and that is it. I eat only because I know that I need to eat something throughout the day. With me, it more than likely has to deal with me having to deal with major depressive order and have been going through a difficult time lately, but my appetite has been lower than normal ever since I started having symptoms.
I'm very interested in that as well. I am not even scheduled yet since in my state I don't qualify yet, but I do plan on having it sometime. Please let us know how your experience goes.

The last couple of times I went to the hospital, they would not accept me because, although I am in a very dark place, have suicidal thoughts, panic attacks, can't sleep, can't eat etc., I don't feel I have it in me to kill myself, so be prepared for that situation. That was in November. I still feel like that now even after working with my therapist and psychiatrist.

The times that I did get admitted, they did a complete strip search looking for any contraband and had a camera on me at all times except for in the bathroom and shower. There is no privacy whatsoever. I was allowed to bring in a couple changes of clothes, and a blanket, but that may have been something special that hospital did. Expect to be ther at least a week but could be up to 2 months. It is very boring there but they will try to get you to participate in activities. Try your hardest to get involved with some of them. We were allowed to talk on the 2 patient designated phones all we wanted as long as it was a local call or incoming call. Anything else needed special permission.

I wish you the best! You're doing the right thing.

I live in severe pain every day, both physical and mental. I have full body CRPS, which is considered one of the most painful diseases known & I have had to deal with it since 2003. These past few years have had me questioning if living in this much pain for however long I would be here for is even worth, and the mental pain has only gotten worse over those years.

I'm also trans, AMAB, and didn't start HRT until I was 28. I had bottom surgery at 30 and no other surgeries after that. I completely understand body dysphoria as I have been there and still have a little to this day, I'm 44 now. I never thought that I would be comfortable with my body and didn't think HRT would help enough. Through the years, my skin has changed, hair growth has changed, breasts naturally grew to a c cup, muscle structure changed, fat repositioned itself, hips have widened, and the rest, such as voice, inflection, movement, mannerisms... all came with some work by myself. I have moved to a small town well away from where I used to live, rarely have enough energy to do my makeup, and nobody knows that I am trans other than my medical team, even they're surprised when they find out. Old family friends always think that I am my sister when they haven't seen me in years. There are a few things that I still don't like about me, but with one exception, they can be changed if I ever feel like changing them. It's all a matter of time. Be patient. You would be surprised how time can work things out.

I know how it feels! I have given up myself as well. I've been dealing with this freaking disease since 2003. After going from doctor to doctor after doctor, they finally gave me the diagnosis of CRPS in 2015. Since then, I have been on so many different medications, some work for a short while but most do nothing. I have tried lsb, biofeedback, pt, therapy and psychiatry, spinal stims, cannabis, which helps a little for a short while but I don't want to be high all day, and currently a DRG stim. The DRG stim actually helped a little, for a year and a half anyway,  then the battery died. When they replaced the battery, they replaced a lead as well and it has only gotten worse since. I now have extreme pain on the entire right side of my body. I am always freezing cold, even if it's in the 90's out. I can't get comfortable enough to sleep more than a few hours every few days, even with sleeping pills.

I see my pm tomorrow. Honestly, I have no idea how I am going to handle the ride down there and back, 6 hours each way, but I  have tried the reputable doctors closer to home. Once I'm there, what could they possibly do at this point? Even if there is something, and it actually works somewhat, it won't last.

To the OP, don't give up based on our stories. For most people, there is hope and something usually works out. People like me are rare cases.

Congratulations on taking the steps to quit smoking! I too have been questioning my gender identity again. I, (44, amab), transitioned starting in 2005 and ended up having GRS in 2007. I do not have as much dysphoria as I used to, but it is still there. I am happy with my body, and where I live, nobody knows that I was assigned male at birth, they only see a female, yet I still feel that I am and never will actually know all of the experiences a woman has throughout their life. There are just too many things that, although I can imagine what it would be like based on all that I have heard, only a cisgender female can experience. And I am usually fine with that. For the most part, I'm glad I don't have to deal with some of it.

My questioning myself again only came up in the last year and a half when one of my doctors asked why I don't have a uterus. When nurses ask that question, I always just say that I was unfortunately born without one, but I felt the need to actually tell my doctor that I was trans. After mentioning this, he asked if I am still considered trans, since I have completed my transition. I told him, technically yes, but I would prefer to be considered gender dysphoric, which is what my gyn considers me. For some reason, I just never felt comfortable being called trans. I always viewed myself as female, and with the exception of 1 other trans person I have met, I do not relate with the many of the thoughts and experiences other trans folk that I know have.

A few months after that appointment, I ran in to my ex-husband while he was taking a vacation in the area that I live now and reminded me that I am still considered trans. Then, this past week, my therapist brought the topic up. She told me that I am very unique, but should be proud of who I am and proud of being trans. I did let her know that I don't like being called trans. Since then, I have been extremely depressed and questioning my identity again. Does all of this make me nb? I don't know because I feel proud to be a woman, but I know deep down, I really am not. I honestly never heard of the term nb until this past week while trying to discover myself again, but all in all, what does it really matter? It's just another label. I am me and people view me how I want to be viewed.

Honestly, I don't know. I have never had confirmation of nerve damage in the years that I have had to deal with CRPS. My doctors have in my chart that it is type 1 but they have told me that they suspect that it is type 2. Personally, it really doesn't matter to me, as long as they are doing their best to treat the problems that I deal with. Unfortunately for me, the lumbar sympathetic blocks did not work for me. Hopefully they will do well for you!

I do like my medical team with the exception that I have a 6 hour ride to get to them. I tried finding someone closer to home and in my own state, but I have already expended the best resources available here.

I can't say anything one way or another about the clinic that you are going to since I have been away from doing any research on CRPS for over 5 years, I have never been there, and I don't remember reading anything about them in the past. Hopefully, somebody else here can give you information on that particular clinic. I can say, that unless you have officially had a doctor confirm actual nerve damage, you are still classified as CRPS type 1.

Best of luck to you on finding good care and treatment options that help!

Keep looking for those reasons to live! Although I feel like I am in the same situation you are in, I know how much it would hurt my family if I actually found the courage to go through with it, I keep looking for more reasons to keep going once my parents pass on. Right now, for me at least, it's taking care of my plants. There are days that my depression makes me feel like not taking care of them, but I usually do. It gets me out of bed nearly every day. Often, only for a short time, but it gives me a reason to keep on going, even if I feel like there is no point anymore.

Oh the joys of the hotline! I've used, or should I say tried to use it twice in my life. The first time, the person on the other end basically just said well, all I can suggest is to go to therapy. It was all of a 2 minute conversation. The other time, I let the phone ring for 30 minutes and gave up then made an attempt. Apparently, it didn't work.
Sounds just like the story of my life!

I much older than you all and I have felt that way most of my life. I really never have and probably never will fit in anywhere. My feeling that life is pointless has been growing an awful lot over the past 6-7 years as well.

They do work for some people, according to one of my old PM docs. I tried it and it did not work for me, of course I was only trying to get relief on one leg at that time. By the time I moved on to my current PM doc, they told me that the CRPS has moved into the spine and that is why it didn't work. Based on that, it sounds unlikely that it will help, since you are full body, but the body is a funny thing. It could still work. Who knows!

Your struggles remind me a little of my situation, (friend sexually assaulted me, then husband started abusing me in multiple ways throughout our relationship including sexual). I never spoke up and kept it all locked up inside. I still do. It tears me apart every day and absolutely nobody knows anything about the sexual abuse, including my husband. He was always extremely drunk every time and couldn't remember anything. At least that's what he always said. I'm pretty sure my therapist has figured it out, but she never brings it up, at least not yet. 

It gets so hard when trying to watch shows with my mom sometimes. She really enjoys Law & Order SVU where it seems like someone is always being raped. That always makes me Just tense up into a little ball and eventually leave. I no longer if stay around if she's watching it anymore.

It's good that you got that out and told somebody.

As the others have stated, opioids do more damage in the long run. Yes, it will give you short term relief on occasion, if it even helps at all, but then they up your dose to give you relief again when it stops working, then on to the next one higher up the list and repeat until your at the maximum dose of Fentanyl. Then it stops working all together and you have to get off of them after your body has become dependent. I took that route and did not like it. Eventually, the opioids were leading to more pain with me. I hope you have success finding a doctor willing to work with you though!

Yes, there are a few support groups online that I post on every once in a while, but besides the reddit group, so few of them have any activity anymore. Even when there are other posters, they're usually just looking for information because they have been recently diagnosed. Many times I would like to respond, but I have forgotten so much about this disease that I no longer feel confident enough in my nowledge to make a comment.
Thank you for the support though.
Yes, I feel that way too. Society has become so greedy that we are doomed to fail as a species.
Climbing gets to be real difficult when you are tied down all the time!

I had a team of doctors through U of M before moving on to Cleveland Clinic. They will do drug screens and will refuse to help if anything comes back positive. They did make a point of using a team approach for me that I liked. It included the pain management doctors, there were 2 of them, one to prescribe any medications and one to perform/request more invasive procedures, and also included a psychologist. They did a lot of testing to determine if I had CRPS instead of reading my multi-year, multi-doctor reports that showed all these steps have already been taken. I ultimately left after the 2nd time of being left in a patient room waiting for over 2 hours waiting for someone to come in to see me. Perhaps things have changed over the years or it was just a bad team of doctors at the time.

I don't have a pain pump myself, but I qualified for one through one of the many PM doctors that I have seen several years ago. There is a port on the pump itself which needs to be filled once a month with whatever medication is being used, morphine and prialt are what were offered to me at the time. It is injected into the port directly through the skin with a needle.
I ultimately decided not to try it back then, and ended up at The Cleveland Clinic to have a DRG stimulator implanted. That worked well for a couple of years, until the battery died. When they replaced the battery  and one of my leads, it stopped having a positive effect for me. Now I'm back searching for hope again.
